title: Court Finds That Using Copyrighted Material as AI Training Data Is Not Fair Use
key_facts: The US Third Circuit Court of Appeals upheld a ruling that Ross Intelligence broke copyright law by training its legal search engine on Thomson Reuters' Westlaw material.
The material at issue was Westlaw 'headnotes', short editorial summaries of legal issues, which Ross effectively copied verbatim.
The original Delaware federal ruling (last year) found Ross's use was not transformative because it was made to build a competing legal research tool.
Ross shut down in 2021, shortly after the suit was filed, citing financial strain from the litigation.
Futurism, citing Reuters, calls it a first-of-its-kind appeals ruling on AI training and fair use.
Ross's remnants have vowed to go to the Supreme Court.
Commentator Aaron Moss (Copyright Lately) says it is not the best vehicle for a sweeping ruling: interlocutory review, damages unresolved, Ross gone, and its AI was not generative.
A hearing in Concord Music Group's suit against Anthropic over song lyrics is scheduled for later this month.
quote_evidence: Last week, a US appeals court upheld a ruling that AI legal research company Ross Intelligence had broken copyright law by training its legal search engine on materials taken from Thomson Reuters' Westlaw legal research platform and database.
"Judging by all the victory laps, you might think everyone had read a different opinion," Moss wrote.
Moss argued that the case isn't the "best vehicle for a sweeping ruling on generative AI."
why_it_matters_hint: First appeals-court ruling on AI training and fair use, but narrow: non-generative AI that copied text verbatim.
event_date: 'Last week' per Futurism (week of 28 Sep 2026; exact date not stated)
notes: Futurism headline says training on copyrighted material is 'not fair use' in general; the article shows a narrower holding. Exact ruling date and judges not stated in the article. Futurism's 'first of its kind' is attributed to Reuters, which was not read.
